data.caption: alevia.com
data.copy:
My brother Dale drove 4 hours through a January blizzard to ask me a question I didn't want to answer.

He pulled into my driveway in Bemidji at 9:47 PM on a Wednesday. The temperature was 11 below. He had ice in his beard. He didn't knock. He used the spare key under the planter and walked into my kitchen and stood there in his Carhartt with the snow melting off his boots onto my linoleum and he looked at me sitting at the table and he said one thing.

He said "why didn't you come."

That's the whole hook of this story. That one question.

But the answer to it is what kept me up that whole night and the next 23 nights after it, and the answer is the reason I'm sitting here typing this on a Saturday morning in May with the windows open and the coffee on and my fingers actually feeling the heat coming off this mug.

My name is Earl. I'm 63 years old. I'm the second of 4 brothers. Our dad worked in the iron mines up in Hibbing for 36 years before they shut down the seam he was on, and he raised us to do 2 things. Work hard. And go fishing.

Specifically, ice fishing.

Every year since 1994, the 4 of us Brennan boys have driven up to Lake of the Woods the second week of January and rented the same set of cabins at the same outfit, Sportsman's Lodge, and spent 4 days drilling holes through 22 inches of ice and pulling walleye out of water so cold it makes your teeth ache.

31 years.

I missed the 32nd.

I told them I had the flu.

I didn't have the flu.

I'm going to back up because the why matters more than the what.

Let me tell you about my feet.

Around 4 years ago, I started getting a little tingling in my toes at night. The kind of pins and needles you get when your foot falls asleep. Except mine didn't go away when I moved them.

I'd lie in bed next to my wife Janet and I'd flex my feet under the covers, and the tingle would just stay there, this low buzz under the skin like someone had left a phone on vibrate inside my shoes.

I didn't tell Janet.

I figured it …

data.caption: rosaliacare.com
data.copy:
My husband finally asked if I was cheating on him.

He didn't say it in anger.

He said it at the kitchen bench at 11pm with a glass of red in his hand and a look on his face I'd never seen before.

"Is there someone else?"

I stood there with a tea towel in my hand and I couldn't speak.

Because the honest answer was no.

And the more honest answer was: how did we get to the point where you had to ask.

========

We've been married 25 years. Together since I was 28.

And the thing about our marriage was that we always gave each other enough space.

We weren't the couple who interrogated each other. We never invaded each other's privacy.

For 25 years that was our strength.

It was about to become the thing that ended us.

========

It had started two years earlier. Slowly.

Sex became something I dreaded.

Everything inside was drier than the Sahara. At first we tried lube, but it did nothing. It sat on top for a couple minutes until the sandpaper rawness feeling came back.

He'd try to be gentle, and I’d hold in the pain. The sting started during and the burning started after. The next morning I'd be on the toilet wincing every time I peed, and that would last 3 days.

By day 4 I was just starting to feel normal again. By day 7 we'd do it again and the countdown would start over.

So I started pulling back. Not all at once. A goodnight kiss instead of a hand on his hip. Going to bed earlier than him. Telling him spooning was uncomfortable.

He noticed. Of course he did.

But he didn't ask.

So he just gave me space. The way he'd been giving me space for 25 years.

========

But here's what I didn't know.

While I was quietly grieving the loss of my own body, my husband was building a theory of his own.

Because from his perspective?

His wife had stopped reaching for him 18 months ago.

data.caption: xarashilajit.com
data.copy:
My neurologist says my Parkinson's medication is working.

And to be fair, he's right.

The tremors are better.

The stiffness is manageable.

My assessment scores haven't gotten dramatically worse.

Every appointment ends the same way.

He reviews the chart.

Looks at the numbers.

Asks a few questions.

Then tells me we're doing well.

The problem is that none of those things explain what my life actually feels like.

Because while my medication was "working," I still felt like I was slowly disappearing.

Not physically.

Mentally.

Emotionally.

The man I used to be was becoming harder to find.

Every day around two in the afternoon it would hit me.

The fog.

The exhaustion.

The feeling that somebody had unplugged my brain and left me running on backup power.

I'd sit in my chair and stare at the television.

Not watching.

Just staring.

My wife would ask me a question and I'd have to think about it longer than I should.

My daughter would call and I'd let it ring because I didn't have the energy for a conversation.

Not because I didn't want to talk to her.

Because keeping up with a conversation had become work.

The worst part wasn't the tremors.

It wasn't the diagnosis.

It was feeling myself become quieter every month.

I used to be the guy who told stories.

The guy who always had something to say.

The guy who could talk for thirty minutes about something nobody else cared about and somehow make it interesting.

Now I'd start a sentence and lose it halfway through.

I'd know exactly what I wanted to say.

I just couldn't get there.

Eventually I stopped trying.

And what scared me most was how normal it became.

My family adjusted.

I adjusted.

My doctors adjusted.

Everyone accepted that this was just part of Parkinson's.

Including me.

Until one night that changed.

A few months ago my daughter sent me an article.

The article talked about a product called Xara 10-in-1 Shilajit Gummies.

Normally I would've ignored it.

I've seen enough supplement …

data.caption: metabolae.com
data.copy:
I almost burned my house down on a Tuesday afternoon in October because I forgot I had put a meatloaf in the oven.

I am 59 years old. My name is Caroline Moore. I am a retired second-grade teacher. I have Type 2 diabetes. I have high blood pressure. I have high cholesterol. My A1C has been between 6.5 and 7.1 for four years. I have been on Metformin, Lisinopril, and Atorvastatin the entire time. My GP has called all three numbers managed at every appointment.

I set the meatloaf in the oven at 4:15. I set the timer on my phone. I went to the living room to sit down for a minute because my legs were tired. At some point I picked up the paperback on the coffee table and started reading. The timer went off. I did not hear it. Or I heard it and it did not register. I do not know which.

My husband came home at 6:20 to a kitchen full of black smoke and a smoke alarm screaming from the ceiling and the meatloaf in the oven turned to charcoal and the oven itself starting to fail.

He turned off the oven. He opened every window in the house. He carried the pan out to the back deck with a dish towel wrapped around his hand.

He came back inside and he stood in the doorway of the living room and he looked at me sitting on the couch with the paperback still open in my lap.

I had not known the timer went off.

I had not smelled the smoke.

I had not heard the alarm.

I looked up at him and I said the sentence that finished four years of me telling myself I was fine.

"George. I did not know."

That night I sat at the kitchen table at 11 PM and I started reading things my doctor had never mentioned in eleven years of appointments.

I had known for about two years that something was wrong.

It started with the words.

I would be in the middle of a sentence at the grocery store or on the phone with my daughter and the word I needed would just not arrive. Not a difficult word. The name of the checkout girl I had known for six years. The word for the thing you use to open cans. My …

She Watched Me Try to Stand Up. She Said: "It's the Way You Brace Before You Move. I Know That Brace. I Used to Have It."

I'm 56.

I had not been to the botanical garden in three years.

I'd been a member since 2011. I'd gone almost every weekend in my forties and early fifties — sometimes with my husband, more often alone. 

It was the place I went when I needed to be reminded that the world was bigger than my office and my house and the inside of my own head.

I'd stopped going sometime in 2022. Not on purpose. The visits had just gotten further apart, and then they'd stopped.

I want to tell you why I went back last May, and what happened on the bench. And then I want to tell you what happened in the year after the bench, which is the actual reason I'm writing this.

I'll back up.

My name is Joanne. I'm 56. I'm a tax accountant. 

I have my own practice with one partner — Bill — and we have three full-time employees. I've been doing this since 1992.

My husband Greg and I have been married twenty-eight years. We have one son, Adam, who's twenty-four and lives in Denver.

I am, by every measure that matters on paper, a healthy woman.

My bloodwork comes back fine. 

My blood pressure is fine. My weight is fine — I'm five-six, I'm 144 pounds, I've been within five pounds of that since college. My cholesterol is fine. 

My A1C is fine. My liver, kidneys, thyroid — all fine.

I have not had a serious illness since I had mono in 1989.

data.copy:
My best friend of 22 years sat me down last Tuesday and asked if I was okay financially.

Not because I’d been shopping too much or missing bills.

Because she thought I’d been getting work done and was worried I was going into debt for procedures.

She’d been quietly tracking how different I looked over the past few months and was ready to lend me money if I needed help.

We were at our usual coffee shop. The one we’ve been meeting at every Tuesday for the past six years.

Sarah ordered her oat milk latte. I ordered my Americano. We sat in our usual booth.

Then she did this thing where she puts her phone face-down on the table.
Our signal for: we need to have a serious conversation.

My first thought: Oh god, who died?
My second thought: Did I forget her birthday again?

She looks at me, very gently, like she’s diffusing a bomb.
“I need to ask you something and I need you to be honest with me.”

I’m thinking: affair, health scare, secret gambling problem—something dramatic.

Then she says:
“How much debt are you in?”

I just stared at her.
“What?”

“For the procedures. I’ve been watching you change over the past few months and I know you’ve been stressed about money and I just—look, I have savings. If you need help paying off a credit card or a medical loan or whatever, I can help. I don’t want you drowning in debt for Botox.”

I legitimately laughed.

Not a polite laugh. A full, unhinged cackle that made the barista look over.

“Sarah. I haven’t had any work done.”

She looked at me like I’d just told her the earth was flat.
“Bullshit.”

“I’m serious. No Botox. No fillers. No lasers. Nothing.”

“Then what the hell have you been doing? Because I’ve literally been taking notes.”

She pulled out her phone and showed me a note titled:
“Tracking [My Name]”
